The Ashvamedha Is Decided

Stories from the Ramayana

The Ashvamedha Is Decided

Rama wishes to perform the Rajasuya — and two old tales change the decision

In everyday English — Uttara Kanda, sargas 83–90

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This book is the story of one decision — and two old tales. First, in the court of Ayodhya, Rama wishes to perform a sacrifice. Then Lakshmana tells an old tale, and Rama tells another old tale. Together the two tales change the decision.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Bharata worried, Lakshmana eager, Indra weary, Ila pleading.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sargas 83–90 — the thought of the Rajasuya, the tale of Vritra, and the tale of King Ila. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — king of Ayodhya. Warm dark-brown skin, plain gold crown, no peacock feather. Now a king, he wishes to perform a great sacrifice.

Bharata — Rama's brother, prince of Ayodhya. He understands both dharma and statecraft, and is not afraid to speak the truth.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother, beside him at every step. Bow in hand, like Rama, a little lighter in complexion.

Indra — king of the gods. About forty years old, thick black moustache, tall gold crown, deep-blue silk robe with a gold border, pearl garland at his throat, golden vajra in his hand.

Vritra — great king of the asuras. An ascetic who knew dharma, but so powerful that even the gods began to fear him.

Vishnu — protector of the gods, whose strength gave Indra his power.

Ila — king of the Bahlika country, son of the Prajapati Kardama. He raised his people as if they were his own children.

Shiva and Uma — the god and goddess of Kailasa. Shiva was playing with Uma in the forest, in a woman's form to please her.

Budha — son of Chandra, the Moon, wise and ascetic, doing penance beside a lake in the forest.

Pururavas — son of Ila and Budha, from whom the Lunar dynasty descends.

Kardama — Ila's father, a Prajapati. Samvarta — a great sage. Marutta — Samvarta's pupil, a king, who performed the Ashvamedha for Ila. Shashabindu — Ila's elder son.

1 · A Question in the Court of Ayodhya · · A QUESTION IN THE COURT OF AYODHYA

There was peace in Ayodhya. Rama was king, the people were happy, and there was no sorrow in the city.

One day Rama sat in the court — Bharata and Lakshmana beside him, ministers and sages seated before him. A thought came to Rama's mind — the thought of performing a great sacrifice.

Rama said — “Brothers, my heart wishes to perform the Rajasuya. The Rajasuya — the greatest sacrifice of kings, by which a king is counted foremost among all kings.”

Silence fell on the court. Then Bharata rose. Bharata always spoke the truth — whether it was sweet or bitter.

Bharata said — “Brother, the Rajasuya means challenging all kings. Any king who does not accept your overlordship must be fought in war. How many kings will die, how many dynasties will be wiped out! Is it dharma to spill so much blood for one sacrifice?”

Rama fell silent. There was weight in Bharata's words. The Rajasuya would bring glory — but its price would be war.

Then Lakshmana spoke — his eyes bright with eagerness.

Lakshmana said — “Brother, there is another sacrifice — the Ashvamedha. It brings just as much glory, but in it no king need be fought in war. A horse is set loose; only the king who stops it gives the challenge. And listen — I will tell you from an old tale how great the power of the Ashvamedha is.”

Rama said — “Tell it, Lakshmana.” — and everyone in the court listened with all their ears.

Pause and think — Rama wants glory — but Bharata says the price of glory must not be war. Does every great deed come only through war? And Lakshmana says — there is another road. Is there only one road to glory, or many?

2 · Who Was Vritra · · WHO WAS VRITRA

Lakshmana said — “Long ago there was a king among the asuras — Vritra.”

Vritra was no ordinary asura. He was an ascetic, he knew dharma, and he wished well for his people. He performed such hard penance that his power kept growing — it grew so great that his name echoed through all three worlds.

The gods began to fear. Indra — king of the gods — feared too. He felt — if Vritra's power grows any further, the rule of the gods itself will totter.

Indra went to Vishnu — the protector of the gods. He said — “Vritra must be stopped, but my strength falls short of his.”

Vishnu said — “Indra, do not fear. My strength will be with you — my power will be in your vajra. Go, and stand for dharma.”

Indra returned — vajra in hand, the strength given by Vishnu in his heart. The gods stood behind him. Before him was Vritra — shining with penance, unmoving as a mountain.

Pause and think — Vritra was not evil — he was an ascetic who knew dharma. Yet the gods feared him. Is power itself the cause of fear — even when that power belongs to a good person? And Indra goes to Vishnu in fear to ask for help — is asking for help in fear also courage?

3 · The Thunderbolt and the Burden of Sin · · THE THUNDERBOLT AND THE BURDEN OF SIN

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of the slaying of Vritra. Elders, please read it gently.

Indra raised the vajra — and struck Vritra. Vritra fell. The gods cried out in triumph — the fear was gone.

But with the victory came a burden. Vritra was born a Brahmin — and the sin of killing him — the sin of brahmahatya — clung to Indra.

Indra's radiance began to fade. The king who once shone like the sun now grew dim. He grew weak, his heart grew heavy, and he began to hide himself from everyone.

A year passed. Indra stayed crushed under the weight of the sin. Then the gods and sages gathered — “Indra must be freed from this burden — or the king of the gods himself will break.”

The sages said — “The sin must be shared. No one alone can carry so heavy a burden.”

The sages said — “Indra, for one year you have carried this burden — now divide it into four parts. The earth will take one part, the waters one, women one, and one part will be taken by those who deceive or kill Brahmins.”

And so it was done. The sin was divided into four parts — the earth took one, the waters one, women one, and deceivers one. With each part came a blessing too — so that those who carried the burden might have some support.

Pause and think — Indra won the victory — but he had to carry the burden of victory too. Does every victory bring a burden with it? And the sages say — share the burden. Does sharing make a burden lighter — or is sharing itself the support?

4 · Indra Is Freed by the Ashvamedha · · INDRA IS FREED BY THE ASHVAMEDHA

The sin was shared — but Indra was not yet fully free. The burden had lightened, but it had not gone.

Then Vishnu said — “Now perform the Ashvamedha. The Ashvamedha — the horse sacrifice — is the sacrifice that washes away even the greatest sin.”

The sages prepared the Ashvamedha. The altar was built, the horse was adorned, mantras echoed. Indra performed the sacrifice — with his heart, with devotion.

The sacrifice was completed — and Indra was freed. His radiance returned — as when the clouds part and the sun shines again. He became king of the gods once more — with a light heart and a clear face.

Lakshmana said — “Brother, see — such is the power of the Ashvamedha. The sacrifice that freed Indra from brahmahatya will be blessed for us too. No war with any king, no dynasty destroyed — only the sacrifice, and glory.”

Rama nodded — Lakshmana's words pleased him. But Rama said — “Lakshmana, you have told Indra's tale. Now I will tell you another tale — the tale of King Ila. It too is a tale of the power of the Ashvamedha.”

Pause and think — Indra found freedom through sacrifice — not through war. Is freedom always won by fighting, or sometimes also through sacrifice, prayer and patience? And hearing Lakshmana's tale, Rama remembers another tale — does one tale call another tale to mind?

5 · King Ila Goes Hunting · · KING ILA GOES HUNTING

Rama said — “Long ago, in the Bahlika country, there was a king — Ila. He was the son of the Prajapati Kardama.”

Ila was a good king. He had brought the whole earth under his hand — not by the sword, but by dharma. He raised his people as if they were his own children. The people honoured him as a father.

One day it was the month of Chaitra — the spring season. Ila went out to hunt — with his foot soldiers and horsemen. He went far into the forest — hunting, chasing, following the game.

Hunting on and on, he reached the place where Kartikeya was born — a holy forest, where waterfalls flowed and flowers bloomed.

In that forest Shiva was playing then — with Uma. Uma — daughter of the mountain — was sporting with Shiva in the forest to please him. Shiva had taken a woman's form to please Uma.

And the rule of that forest was this — while Shiva played there with Uma, no male there remained a male — every creature there became a woman.

Pause and think — Ila was a good king — but following the hunt he wandered into a forest whose rule he did not know. Can even a good man make a mistake without knowing? And the rule of the forest — does every place have its own rules, which we should learn first?

6 · The Change in the Forest · · THE CHANGE IN THE FOREST

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of Ila becoming a woman. Elders, please read it gently.

Ila entered the forest — and saw — the animals, the birds, the trees there — all were in a woman's form. Then he looked at himself — he too had become a woman! His soldiers with him — all had become women.

Ila was afraid. He understood — “This is the doing of Shiva, the lord of Uma.”

Ila went with his companions to Shiva — and fell at his feet. He pleaded — “Lord, give me back my form as a man.”

Shiva laughed — and Uma laughed with him. Shiva said — “Rise, royal sage, son of Kardama. Ask for anything you like — only do not ask for your manhood. That one thing I will not give.”

The one thing Ila had asked for, Shiva refused. So Ila turned from Shiva — and fell at the feet of the goddess Uma.

Ila said — “Goddess, have mercy on me.”

Uma said — “Shiva will grant half of your wish, and I will grant the other half. Tell me — how will you have it?”

Ila said — “Then let me be a woman for one month, and a man for the next.”

Uma said — “So be it. But hear one thing — as a man you will not remember the woman, and as a woman you will not remember the man.”

The boon was given — half and half. For one month Ila was a woman, the next month a man.

Pause and think — Shiva refused Ila's greatest wish — but Uma found a way. When one door closes, can there be another door too? And Ila asked for half and half — is receiving half also receiving?

7 · Budha and Pururavas · · BUDHA AND PURURAVAS

In the first month Ila — in a woman's form — left her chariots behind and wandered on foot through the forest with her companions. They reached a mountain — there was a lake there, full of birds.

In the lake stood Budha — son of Chandra, the Moon. He was doing hard penance standing in the water — his face shone like the rising moon. But when he saw Ila — he could no longer stand still in the water.

When the women came out of the lake, Budha called them to his hermitage.

Budha asked — “Who is this lady, and why has she come here?”

The companions said — “She is our mistress. She has no husband. She wanders the woods with us.”

Budha meditated and learned the whole tale of Ila. Then he said to the companions — “Live on this mountain as kimpurusha women — eat roots, leaves and fruit, and kimpurusha men will be your husbands.” — and they went to live on the slopes of the mountain.

Ila stayed in Budha's hermitage. One month passed in the blink of an eye — and Ila woke again as a man — remembering nothing.

Ila asked — “Where have my people gone?”

Budha said — “While you slept a storm of hail came — and swept them away. Stay here in peace.”

Ila said — “I cannot stay — I have a kingdom, I have a home. My elder son Shashabindu will be king after me.”

Budha said — “Son of Kardama, stay one year — do not grieve. At the end of it I will grant you a boon.”

Ila stayed for one year. One month she lived with Budha as a woman, the next month as a man she kept to her duties. In the ninth month she gave birth to a son — Pururavas, the very image of his father — and placed the child in Budha's arms.

The year was complete. Now the worry over her form as a man troubled Ila again — would she ever become fully a man again?

Pause and think — Ila is a woman for one month, a man for the next — and each month forgets the last. Is forgetting also part of the boon? And Budha helps Ila — asking nothing in return. Is help always given to get something back?

8 · The Ashvamedha Brings Him Back · · THE ASHVAMEDHA BRINGS HIM BACK

When the year was complete Budha called the great sages together — Samvarta, Chyavana, Durvasa and other sages came. Ila's father Kardama came too.

Kardama said — “Only Shiva can set Ila right. And no sacrifice is dearer to Shiva than the Ashvamedha.”

So King Marutta — Samvarta's pupil — performed the Ashvamedha beside Budha's hermitage. The altar was built, the horse was adorned, mantras echoed, the fire burned.

Shiva was pleased — and he gave Ila back his manhood — completely, for ever.

Ila gave the Bahlika country to his elder son Shashabindu — and built a new city in the middle land — Pratishthana. When Ila's time was complete, Pururavas — Budha's son — ruled in Pratishthana.

Rama said — “See, brothers — such is the power of the Ashvamedha. It freed Indra from sin — and it gave Ila back his form. The sacrifice that can save even a god, and even a king — that is the sacrifice I will perform.”

Pause and think — Ila got his form back through a sacrifice — not through any war. Is a lost thing always won back by fighting — or sometimes also through sacrifice, prayer and the help of sages? And Ila gave his old kingdom to his son and built a new city — is beginning anew also a return?

9 · The Decision Is Made · · THE DECISION IS MADE

Both tales had been heard — Indra's tale, and Ila's tale. There was silence in the court — then Rama rose.

Rama said — “Bharata, your words were right — in the Rajasuya there would be war, and I do not want glory through war. Lakshmana, your words were right too — in the Ashvamedha there is glory, and there is peace. My decision is firm — I will perform the Ashvamedha.”

Bharata smiled — Lakshmana bowed his head. The sages and ministers rejoiced — cries of “Sadhu! Sadhu!” rose from all sides.

Rama said — “Call the sages — send invitations to holy men from every land. Let the preparations for the sacrifice begin. The horse will be set loose — and wherever it goes, Rama's name will go with it.”

The court rose — but the tale was not yet over. The horse of the Ashvamedha will be set loose, sages will come, and two boys will come to that sacrifice — who will sing Rama's own tale.

But that story — is in the next book.

Pause and think — Rama set aside the Rajasuya and chose the Ashvamedha — hearing Bharata's warning, and hearing two old tales. Is a good decision taken alone — or by listening, thinking, and accepting the words of others? And Rama's decision — is it only the decision of a sacrifice, or the decision to win glory in peace?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sargas 83–90.

The Thought of the Rajasuya — Sarga 83

Rama's thought of performing the Rajasuya; Bharata saying that the Rajasuya means challenging all kings and war; Lakshmana proposing the Ashvamedha instead — this is in sarga 83.

The Tale of Vritra — Sargas 84–86

Vritra as an ascetic asura king; Indra striking with the vajra by Vishnu's strength; the sin of brahmahatya clinging to Indra; the sin divided into four parts — earth, waters, women, and those who deceive or kill Brahmins; and Indra's freedom through the Ashvamedha — this is in sargas 84–86.

The Tale of Ila — Sargas 87–90

Ila, son of Kardama and king of Bahlika, hunting into the forest where Shiva plays in a woman's form to please Uma; all becoming women; Uma's half-and-half boon — one month a woman, one month a man; meeting Budha and the birth of Pururavas; Marutta's Ashvamedha and Shiva's return of Ila's manhood; Bahlika to Shashabindu and the founding of the city of Pratishthana — this is in sargas 87–90.

About the Other Tellings

The tale of Ila also appears in the Matsya Purana and other texts — there Ila is told as the son of Manu, and some details differ. This book follows only the tale as told in the Ramayana — Ila is the son of Kardama, king of Bahlika.

About the Pictures

No picture in this book shows the slaying of Vritra — only the gods' worry, Indra's faded radiance, and the fire of the sacrifice are shown. The picture of Ila's change too shows only the pleading — Ila with folded hands before Shiva and Uma. There is no blood, no wound, no frightening scene anywhere.

What Happens Next

The horse of the Ashvamedha will be set loose — and Lava and Kusha will come to that sacrifice and sing Rama's tale. That story is in the next books of this series.
